speaker: gizmo
text: Scientists look very closely. Let’s spot what makes each shark special!

speaker: gizmo
text: Which shark has a wide, hammer-shaped head?

speaker: gizmo
text: The hammerhead! Its wide head has special sensors that help it find food.

speaker: gizmo
text: Which shark has pale spots all over its back?

speaker: gizmo
text: The whale shark! It is the biggest fish in the sea.

speaker: gizmo
text: Which shark has a long, flat snout?

speaker: gizmo
text: The goblin shark! Its flat snout helps it search for food in the deep.

speaker: gizmo
text: Which shark has a big dark spot behind its fin?

speaker: gizmo
text: The epaulette shark! That dark spot helps us recognise it.

speaker: gizmo
text: Which shark has a pointed nose and a strong tail for speed?

speaker: gizmo
text: The mako! Its pointed nose and strong tail help it swim fast, like Dash.

speaker: gizmo
text: Fish have fins and breathe with gills. Let’s sort the sea animals!

speaker: gizmo
text: A tuna. Is it a fish?

speaker: gizmo
text: Yes! A tuna has fins and breathes with gills.

speaker: gizmo
text: Fish, or Not a fish?

speaker: gizmo
text: A crab. Is it a fish?

speaker: gizmo
text: Not a fish! A crab has legs and a hard shell, and no fins.

speaker: gizmo
text: A whale shark. Is it a fish?

speaker: gizmo
text: Yes! A whale shark is a fish, even with whale in its name. It breathes with gills.

speaker: gizmo
text: A sea turtle. Is it a fish?

speaker: gizmo
text: Not a fish! Sea turtles breathe air with lungs. They are reptiles.

speaker: gizmo
text: A clownfish. Is it a fish?

speaker: gizmo
text: Yes! A clownfish has fins and gills.

speaker: gizmo
text: A dolphin. Is it a fish?

speaker: gizmo
text: Not a fish! Dolphins breathe air, like us. They are mammals.

speaker: gizmo
text: Scientists guess first, then test. Will it sink or float? Make your guess!

speaker: gizmo
text: Sharks don’t sink to the bottom when they swim. Most sharks have a big, oily liver that helps them stay up in the water.

text: A rock. Will it sink or float?

text: It floats! Wood floats, and the boat’s shape helps too.

text: A sea shell. Will it sink or float?

speaker: gizmo
text: It sank to the bottom, where shells are found on the sea floor.

text: Sea animals move in different ways. How does each one move?

text: Millions of years ago, long before people. It disappeared about 3.6 million years ago. Extinct means none are alive today.

text: It ate large sea animals, including whales. Fossil bones sometimes show tooth marks.

text: Scientists study huge fossil teeth and other remains, including some backbone fossils. Its name means “big tooth”.

text: No! It is a fish. Like other sharks, it breathes through gills. Whales breathe air with lungs.

text: Tiny animals called plankton, and small fish. It filters food from the water.

text: In many seas around the world, including around Australia.

speaker: gizmo
text: Fish and other sea animals. Larger great whites also eat seals.

speaker: gizmo
text: A dark back and light belly help it blend in when seen from above or below. This is called countershading.

speaker: gizmo
text: It moves its tail from side to side. Its fins help it balance and steer.

text: Scalloped hammerhead.

speaker: gizmo
text: Its wide head has special sensors that help it find food. Its eyes sit near the ends.

speaker: gizmo
text: Fish, squid and rays. Young sharks often eat smaller food.

speaker: gizmo
text: Sometimes. Scalloped hammerheads can also gather in big groups called schools.
